messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nia had been a police officer for nearly a decade, the kind of woman her family in Atlanta described as steady and unshakable, until a late-night call after a traffic stop changed the way she moved through the world. She had gone alone to speak with a man who had become agitated outside a convenience store, assuming it would be another difficult but manageable encounter. Instead, he forced her into a back room, and what followed was a sexual assault she still could not bring herself to describe in full. In the months afterward, Nia found that parts of the event remained frustratingly blank no matter how hard she tried to piece them together; she would circle the same missing stretches in her mind, feeling ashamed of the gaps and furious at herself for not being able to remember every detail. At other moments the memory came back with brutal force, and when it did she felt a sharp, real pain in the same parts of her body that had been hurt that night, as if her body had never fully left the room. Along with that came a hot, consuming rage that startled her with its intensity and left her ashamed afterward.

What troubled Nia most was not only what had happened, but what it seemed to say about her. She had come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, that another officer would have seen the danger sooner, handled the man differently, or found a way out before the assault happened. She told herself that she had permanently changed for the worse, that the version of her who used to laugh easily with her sisters, move comfortably through neighborhood events, and feel rooted in her community was gone. She also felt that she had lost her connection to her community and culture; the familiar rhythms of cookouts, church gatherings, and family celebrations no longer felt like home in the same way, because she experienced herself as separate from the people around her, as if something essential had been cut away. Those beliefs made it hard for her to bear ordinary emotion at all. If anger, sadness, or fear began to rise, she backed away from whatever was provoking it, certain that strong feelings would overwhelm her and expose just how damaged she had become. She did the same with conflict, avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even at work, where she began volunteering for paperwork, administrative tasks, and quieter shifts whenever she could.

The memory kept shaping those choices. A radio call, the smell of stale food in a convenience store, or even a sudden surge of pain in her back or hips could bring the assault rushing into the room with her, and once it did she would spend hours trying to push it away, often by numbing herself to anything that stirred too much feeling. She found herself avoiding hard conversations with her husband, stepping out of family gatherings early, and declining invitations from relatives whose questions might lead to tears or anger. At work, she became careful not to challenge colleagues, not to press a point, and not to walk into disagreements that once would have felt routine. The more she withdrew from situations that made her feel too much, the more alone she felt in her own life, and the more convinced she became that she had already lost the person and community she used to be. Even when she was not actively recalling the attack, the sense of permanent damage lingered, quiet but constant, making every strong feeling seem like proof that she was no longer the same woman.

By the time she came to therapy, Nia was exhausted by the effort of keeping herself contained. She said she had finally sought help after realizing she was running her whole life around the assault, at home and in her precinct, and that the pattern was leaving her isolated from her husband, distant from her family, and less confident on the job. What frightened her most was that the rage and pain would keep returning whenever the memory broke through, and that if she let herself feel too much she would fall apart or lash out. What she hoped for, though she could barely say it aloud, was a way to remember without being overwhelmed, and to believe that the woman she had been was not entirely lost.
